A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SMITE, with matching authors, method and core experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support reliable comparison; the embedded Figure 3 animation is unchanged.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation results on SMITE-50, PUMaVOS and PASCAL-Part, component ablations and a 40-participant user study.

after.justification: V2 retains original segmentation experiments and adds DAVIS evaluations, further ablations and generalization examples, alongside a revised 25-participant user study.

M1.justification: The inflated U-Net, two-phase embedding/cross-attention training, bidirectional temporal voting, low-pass regularization and latent optimization already appear in v1. V2 clarifies these components and their losses. The long-video revision concerns chunk and overlap settings within the existing processing scheme.

E1.justification: V2 adds DAVIS-2016 single-object segmentation in zero-shot and semi-supervised settings. It also demonstrates horse-to-camel/giraffe transfer, sedan-to-SUV transfer and mixed horse/car segmentation (Figures 10–11). SMITE-50, selected PUMaVOS sequences and PASCAL-Part remain.

E2.justification: V2 adds Baseline-II (SLiMe plus CoTracker) and Baseline-III (SLiMe with an inflated U-Net) to both the SMITE-50 comparison and user study. New DAVIS tables compare against twelve zero-shot and ten semi-supervised methods, including FSNet, OAST, STM and XMem. Existing PUMaVOS and image-segmentation comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Car-only component and few-shot ablations become evaluations across SMITE-50. The user study retains 16 videos but changes from 40 to 25 participants and from three to five methods. New DAVIS protocols use training-set reference frames or one frame per evaluated video, reporting both all 20 videos and an 18-video subset. Long-video chunk/overlap settings are also revised.

E4.justification: V1's separate car-only loss and cross-attention ablations are replaced by a cumulative, full-dataset component ablation. V2 adds joint-versus-two-phase training analysis, training-stability curves, postprocessing-versus-inference tracking comparisons, cross-category and multi-object case studies, and thin-structure failure examples (Table 8; Figures 9–13).

E5.justification: V2 adds Levene's variance test for the training-strategy comparison (p = 0.0036) and mean validation-loss curves with standard-deviation shading in Figure 9. This statistical reporting is confined to the added analysis; repeated-run counts and the sampling basis of the shading remain unspecified.

E6.justification: Retained category scores in Table 1, PUMaVOS results and PASCAL-Part results are unchanged. V2 adds baseline results, joint-versus-two-phase mIoU of 62.17 versus 75.14, and DAVIS results, including full-set SMITE J/F of 80.8/82.9 and 83.4/80.7 in the two settings. Car-only few-shot scores 63.03/71.55/75.10 are replaced by full-dataset scores 58.55/73.88/75.14. User-study scores also change under the revised design, preventing direct performance comparisons.

T1.justification: The substantive mathematics in Equations 1–8 and the optimization description is retained. Appendix 7.6 expands the existing WAS computation and inherited SLiMe losses into explicit formulas, without introducing new theoretical assumptions, proofs or mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and contribution statements retain the same central claims: reference-guided video segmentation with flexible granularity, temporal consistency, cross-attention tuning and the SMITE-50 benchmark. Added experiments support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: V2 expands applicability and mechanism discussion through cross-category transfer, training stability and the distinction between tracking during optimization and postprocessing. It explains why low-pass regularization is not separately ablated without tracking. The limitations now explicitly cover tracker dependence, low-resolution attention causing fine-detail failures, and the inability to provide interactive segmentation; DAVIS failure cases make these boundaries concrete.

D1.justification: V2 newly documents 300 training epochs, batch-size and memory tradeoffs, 20-minute training reducible to seven minutes, and 26-second-per-frame inference. Appendix 7.6 details WAS and loss computation. Long-video documentation changes from 20-frame chunks retaining seven WAS maps to configurable 2T-frame chunks retaining T+1 states. Most earlier implementation details and pseudocode remain.

R1.justification: Additional citations support the DAVIS comparisons and dataset context, including FSNet, TMO, OAST, STM and AOT. These extend the comparison literature, while Section 2 and the central novelty positioning remain essentially unchanged. Duplicate entries for already cited works do not establish additional research coverage.

P1.justification: V2 clarifies selected preliminaries and tracking paragraphs, expands the limitations, adds acknowledgements and a WAS explanation, and reorganizes appendix subsections. Most of the abstract, introduction and method narrative is retained, so this is a focused editorial expansion.

P2.justification: Table 1 gains comparator rows and mean columns; the separate component tables become a cumulative ablation display. V2 adds dataset, training-strategy and DAVIS tables, plus Figures 8–13 covering mechanisms, stability, generalization and failures. Existing Figure 7 is reformatted, while v1's challenging-case Figure 8 moves to appendix Figure 14.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially strengthens validation of the central design choices: Baselines II/III, the full-dataset component ablation and the controlled training comparison address alternatives insufficiently tested in v1. DAVIS results and concrete failure examples also clarify applicability. These gains outweigh the smaller user study and limited reporting defects, including Baseline-I's inconsistent 66.62 versus 66.22 mIoU in Tables 1–2. The improvement comes from stronger evidence and clearer boundaries, not higher retained benchmark scores.
